1.pericope_label: He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily. For the Lord hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the four short orders sententious and of course ironical, comparing the directions given to the priests of the false god on the mountain, and thinks the man who dashes in pieces may be the Median king; on the second verse he renders that the Lord restores the glory of Jacob so that it is as the glory of ancient Israel, and resolves the construction by weighing the two names, the first the birth-name of a homeless and downtrodden people and the second the name God gave the man who prevailed, while rejecting the alternative that the two stand for the two kingdoms. Keil and Delitzsch render with the turning away and pass on to the advancing army.

Gill rejects the reading that makes this the Assyrian coming against Jerusalem, ascribing it to one Jewish commentator, and follows another in making it the Babylonian, not the famous king of that name but his father, who joined the Mede in taking the city; on the second verse he takes the clause as a reckoning for the insolence of two Assyrian kings against the two kingdoms. Calvin sets out three constructions of the first verse and prefers the last, and on the second argues that the noun is far more often used in a bad sense, of haughtiness, so that the meaning is that the time was ripe for the fall of the city because God had already humbled his own people.

Clarke names the Median and Babylonian kings as the destroyers and calls the chapter a set-piece of Hebrew poetry, giving the muster of the armies, the siege, the flooding of the river and the sack; on the second verse he reports a bishop's emendation that the Lord restores but does not see that much is gained by it, keeping to the plain sense that the Lord had been opposed to Jacob and the enemy had prevailed. Wesley says only that the destroyers are Medes or Chaldeans.

Henry makes the destroyer the Babylonian and reports that the word may equally be rendered scatter; he writes the irony of the four orders out at length, bidding them secure the towers and magazines, set guards on the avenues, encourage the soldiers and fortify as cities do when an enemy advances, and still the stroke will not be put by, since there is no counsel or strength against the Lord.

debates.question: Who is the destroyer, and whom do the four orders address?

positions.position: Three readings are possible: the waster has vanished and the orders are a comfort to Judah; or they are a terror spoken during a siege; or the address is to the Assyrians and the destroyer is the Babylonian.
The Babylonian king's father with the Mede, against Nineveh, not the Assyrian against Jerusalem.
The orders are ironical, and the man who dashes in pieces may be the Median king.
The Babylonian, addressed to Nineveh, with the orders written out as irony.

debates.question: Does the second verse say that the Lord turned away the glory of Jacob or that he restores it?

positions.position: Turned away: the noun means haughtiness, and the sense is that God had first humbled his own people.
Restores: the Lord makes the glory of Jacob as the glory of ancient Israel.
The emendation to restores is reported but not adopted; the Lord had been opposed to Jacob and the enemy prevailed.
Rendered with the turning away, without comment.

outliers.claim: Reads the first verse on one construction as saying the waster has VANISHED rather than ascended, so that the four orders become a comfort to the chosen people: let every man return to his city, look out which way the invader came and find it clear, and stand firm, the monarchy that oppressed them being now to be cut off.

themes: He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily.
For the Lord hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches.

3.pericope_label: The shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men are in scarlet: the chariots shall be with flaming torches in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken. The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings. He shall recount his worthies: they shall stumble in their walk; they shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the mighty men are the besieger's, takes the redness to be blood and rules out the bright red copper of which shields were made, renders that the chariots are equipped with flashing steel and inclines to take it of scythes fixed to the wheels, renders the cypress lances as brandished, restricts the raging chariots to the besieged city, and presses the last clause to mean that the storming-shed has already been set against the wall. Keil and Delitzsch keep the metal, rendering the chariots as in the fire of the steel-bosses.

Gill takes the mighty men for the soldiers of Babylon and Media and offers three explanations of the redness without choosing between them, the blood of the slain, a dye laid on to inject terror, or the glitter of gilded metal; on the raging chariots he takes them for the enemy's, driven through the streets of the captured city, while reporting a Jewish reading that makes them the defenders' own; and on the mustering he again gives both possibilities. Calvin dismisses as too strained the reading that makes the described army Assyrian, reports that the word for the chariots' fire occurs nowhere else and concludes that lamps are meant, and takes the shaken trees for lances trembling in the soldiers' hands.

Clarke goes against the others in referring the red shields and scarlet clothing to the preparations of the besieged, takes the shaken trees for darts, arrows and javelins flung with destructive power, and has both sets of chariots meeting in the streets.

debates.question: Whose army is described in the third verse?

positions.position: The besieger's.
The besieged Ninevites' own preparations.
The Chaldeans; the reading that makes them Assyrians is too strained.

debates.question: What is the obscure word in the clause about the chariots?

positions.position: Flashing steel, perhaps scythes fixed to the wheels; the older Hebrew commentators rendered it torches.
Lamps or torches; the word occurs nowhere else and its letters may have been inverted.
The fire of the steel-bosses.

outliers.claim: Reports a stranger account of the red shields, that they were painted so that blood should not show and the soldiers clothed in red so that they should not be frightened by their own wounds, which he says is recorded of an ancient people; but the habits of these nations being little known, he declines to decide.

themes: The shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men are in scarlet: the chariots shall be with flaming torches in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken.
The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings.
He shall recount his worthies: they shall stumble in their walk; they shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared.

6.pericope_label: The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved. And Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts. But Nineveh is of old like a pool of water: yet they shall flee away. Stand, stand, shall they cry; but none shall look back. Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the gates of the rivers as the dams fencing the stream that ran through the city and the river outside, holds the ancient account of the fall inaccurate in detail but founded on fact, takes the verb rendered dissolved in its literal sense of a solid dissolved by water against a modern figurative reading, rejects the proper name in the seventh verse in favour of a verb meaning that it is decided, and prefers a slight change of reading in the eighth by which her waters are like a pool and the inhabitants are fleeing. Keil and Delitzsch keep the name and render that she is led away captive.

Gill takes the gates of the rivers three ways, as two named streams, the gates nearest the great river, or the river itself which broke down two miles and a half of wall; he reports most of the readings of the disputed name, from the Targum's queen to the palace and the city itself; and he takes the pool for a place as full of people as a pool of fish, full also of unstable wealth and undisturbed from the beginning. Calvin makes the gates a rhetorical point, that side being best defended and the prophet ridiculing a confidence that thought enemies wholly shut out there; he calls the proper-name reading too strained and refers the words to the state of the kingdom by personification; and he makes the pool an answer to the objection that antiquity lends kingdoms strength and authority.

Clarke rests the verse on the ancient account of the oracle, the swollen river, the twenty stadia of fallen wall and the king's self-immolation, and reads that as the literal fulfilment, taking the dissolving of the palace to mean that it was burnt; he inclines to make the disputed name the queen, since the account of the burning names only the king, the concubines and the eunuchs; and he reports a bishop's rendering that the waters of the city are a pool of waters, referring it to the inundation.

debates.question: What does it mean that the palace is dissolved?

positions.position: That it was burnt, as the ancient account of the king's pyre describes.
Literally, a solid dissolved by water; the figurative reading of it as the dissolution of the empire is refused.
The fortresses melt of themselves, as though the walls were paper and the stones water.

debates.question: What is the disputed word usually left untranslated in the seventh verse?

positions.position: A queen, or the queen's own name; others make it the king figured as a woman, an idol, the palace, or the city.
The queen, who may be supposed to have escaped the burning.
Not a name at all but a verb: it is decided.
The proper-name reading is too strained; the words refer by personification to the state of the kingdom.
The name is kept and she is led away captive.

outliers.claim: Makes the pool an answer to an objection nobody else raises, that antiquity lends kingdoms both strength and authority, so that a people who boasted they had always been, as another nation fabled its kingdom older than the world, could not believe there would be an end where there was no beginning.

themes: The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved.
And Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts.
But Nineveh is of old like a pool of water: yet they shall flee away. Stand, stand, shall they cry; but none shall look back.
Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture.

10.pericope_label: She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness. Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions, where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion’s whelp, and none made them afraid? The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin. Behold, I am against thee, saith the Lord of hosts, and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions: and I will cut off thy prey from the earth, and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers a withdrawal of brightness to a gathering of blackness in the faces, referring the reader to the same expression in an earlier prophet. Keil and Delitzsch render the last verse plainly, the chariots burned in smoke and the sword devouring the young lions.

Gill says the three opening terms are heaped up to confirm the thing and that there is an elegant play here which English cannot express; he names four Assyrian kings as the lions; he leaves the text at the twelfth verse to report an old opinion that the lioness bears but once in her life and then but one, refuted by a later writer out of two ancient authorities; and he records the alternative rendering that God will come to Nineveh rather than be against her. Calvin makes the change of speaker at the last verse the point, since God declaring his own decree without the mouth of a man is far more impressive, and rejects the suggestion that the smoke means no more than a smoky fire.

Clarke shows what the play on the three words consists in, that they are of the same sound and grow longer as they go, so their very shape marks a desolation great, greater and greatest; he takes the blackness of the faces for a real change of complexion brought on by famine; he assigns each term of the lion allegory its counterpart, whelps, lionesses, holes and dens standing for sons, queen, treasure-houses and wardrobes, and calls it a very fine allegory admirably supported; and he closes on the voice that shall be heard no more.

Henry presses the lion comparison until it turns against the men described: cruel tyrants are worse than the beasts they are likened to, since being men humanity is expected of them and lions do not prey on their own kind, yet these walked in their city as a lion in the woods, feared by everybody and loved by nobody. He turns the tearing and strangling into a domestic excuse and refuses it, and finds contempt in the odd preposition of the last verse, since it is not said in the fire but in the smoke.

debates.question: What does the burning of the chariots in the smoke mean?

positions.position: Not a smoky fire: at the first onset the whole force of the city is consumed, chariots standing for every kind of warlike preparation.
Contempt: not in the fire but in the smoke, consumed while the fire has not yet flamed out; or else the drivers are smothered where they sit.
Rendered plainly, the chariots burned in smoke and the sword devouring the young lions.

debates.question: What happens to the faces of them all?

positions.position: A real change of complexion, the diseased look brought on by famine.
Not a gathering of blackness but a withdrawal of brightness.

outliers.claim: Leaves the text at the twelfth verse to settle a point of natural history, reporting the old opinion that the lioness bears but once in her life and then but one, noting that a later writer refuted it out of two ancient authorities, and adding that the prophet's own words disprove it.

themes: She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness.
Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions, where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion’s whelp, and none made them afraid?
The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin.

Behold, I am against thee, saith the Lord of hosts, and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions: and I will cut off thy prey from the earth, and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard.
